question: Can an interaction energy built from a vanishing mollifier turn sampling from an unnormalized target into practical first-order particle optimization, including when every sample must satisfy differentiable constraints?

key_findings.claim: The paper's exact convergence identity is missing the normalization constant of the target and is false for the unnormalized densities allowed by its setup.
key_findings.evidence: The setup defines Z = integral_X p and mu* with density p/Z, but Theorem 3.3 and Lemma A.8 identify the MIE limit integral q(x)^2/p(x) dx with chi-square(mu||mu*)+1. Direct substitution gives chi-square(mu||mu*)+1 = Z times integral q^2/p, so the displayed MIE limit is actually (chi-square+1)/Z. Rescaling p changes E_epsilon but cannot change chi-square, making the contradiction immediate. The same factor propagates to the Gamma-limit and the claimed limiting minimum value 1, although it does not change the minimizer or log-energy gradient.

anchors.section: Lemma A.8 and proof of Theorem 3.3

key_findings.claim: After correcting that scale factor, the central variational construction still supports the intended target minimizer in its stated regular regime.
key_findings.evidence: For a measure with density q and finite chi-square divergence, mollifier convolution sends the MIE to integral q^2/p. With i.s.p.d. translation kernels, the energy is strictly convex on compact X; the Fourier/Bochner argument establishes Gamma-convergence, and compactness then sends continuous-energy minimizers weakly to the normalized target. The result concerns continuous measures and an epsilon-to-zero limit, not finite-particle optimization rates.

key_findings.claim: The practical MIED update is a differentiable log-sum-exp particle objective with flexible constraint adapters, but its nearest-neighbor diagonal rule is an additional heuristic beyond the continuous theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The discrete energy weights each pair by phi_epsilon(x_i-x_j)/sqrt(p(x_i)p(x_j)), optimizes its logarithm, and replaces each singular diagonal value with phi_epsilon(h_i/kappa_n), where h_i is the nearest-neighbor distance. Reparameterization handles mapped domains, while dynamic-barrier projection handles differentiable inequalities and uses 20 Dykstra sweeps for multiple constraints. The finite-N justification is asymptotic and supplies neither a finite-particle error nor an optimization convergence rate.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact does not exactly implement the manuscript's bandwidth or modified-diagonal gradient conventions, and one advertised diagonal mode is reversed.
key_findings.evidence: At commit df408d263774a693e0f0eb62ccdc9f1a26921827, the Riesz code computes (distance_squared + eps)^(-s/2), whereas the paper defines (distance_squared + epsilon^2)^(-s/2); thus the default code value eps=1e-8 corresponds to mathematical epsilon=1e-4, not the paper's stated epsilon=1e-8. The Gaussian code has the same variance-versus-standard-deviation convention. For nnd_scale, the nearest-neighbor squared distance is detached, so updates are not gradients of the displayed configuration-dependent diagonal energy. The include_diag='ignore' branch selects only diagonal entries; a two-particle smoke check returned zero gradient, while the default experiments use nnd_scale and avoid this branch. The code also omits the manuscript's additive -2 log N term, affecting logged energy values but not gradients.

key_findings.claim: The strongest theoretical optimization statements have incompatible assumptions under the paper's own global setup.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.5 fixes X=R^n and the setup requires p(x)>0 everywhere, but Proposition 3.8 assumes p is compactly supported, which cannot hold simultaneously for a nonzero target. Assumption A.21 instead requires p >= 1/C_p everywhere on R^n, which makes integral p infinite and contradicts the setup's finite normalizer. Consequently the displacement-convexity statement and discrete-time descent lemma do not directly apply to any probability target admitted by the global R^n setup without reformulating the domain or assumptions.

key_findings.claim: The experiments support competitiveness and constraint flexibility rather than uniform superiority.
key_findings.evidence: MIED improves high-dimensional Gaussian W2 distance while SVGD has lower energy distance; it captures the tested heavy-tailed Student distribution where SVGD fails. In the 13 Bayesian-logistic datasets, MIED has the lowest displayed logarithmic W2 distance in 8 rows and the lowest logarithmic energy distance in 4, with accuracy largely insensitive to posterior quality. For box-uniform sampling it beats the shown alternatives, while Appendix D.4 explicitly reports that SVMD and MSVGD can outperform it on the 20-dimensional Dirichlet problem when a good mirror map is available. The fairness plot shows a larger empirical Pareto front but gives no uncertainty bars or numeric table.

method.core_idea: Approximate a density-ratio quadratic functional with a short-range pairwise kernel, then optimize its empirical log energy so attraction to high target density and repulsion between particles arise from one scalar objective.
method.mechanism: Define W_epsilon(x,y)=phi_epsilon(x-y)/sqrt(p(x)p(y)); descend the log-sum-exp of all particle-pair interactions; regularize diagonal interactions using nearest-neighbor spacing; and compose the update with a differentiable reparameterization or a dynamic-barrier projection for constraints.
assumptions: The target is positive and continuously differentiable on a closed full-dimensional domain and has a finite normalizer.
The mollifier is symmetric, normalized, bounded, and concentrates at zero in both L1 and L-infinity tails.
Strict convexity and Gamma-limit conclusions require the associated translation kernel to be i.s.p.d.; convergence of minimizers additionally uses compactness of X.
Theorem 3.3 applies only to candidate measures with finite chi-square divergence, while gradient calculations impose smooth compact-support conditions on the candidate density and mollifier.
The finite-particle argument is a sequential asymptotic in N and epsilon and does not guarantee that the nonconvex particle optimizer reaches a global discrete minimizer.
The displayed normalization identities implicitly require Z=1 despite the setup allowing unnormalized p; otherwise the corrected factor 1/Z is necessary.

techniques.role: Turns an inaccessible density-ratio quadratic into a pairwise interaction integral using an approximate identity.
Removes arbitrary multiplicative normalizers from gradient dynamics and stabilizes extreme short-range interactions.
Replaces singular self-interactions with values determined by nearest-neighbor spacing.
Handles mapped domains by reparameterization and generic differentiable inequalities by projected dynamic-barrier directions.
Uses positive Fourier spectra, Plancherel, and compactness to connect continuous-energy minimizers to the target.

evaluations.setting: Skewed Gaussians over dimensions and particle counts, averaged over 10 trials.
evaluations.metric: Wasserstein-2 distance and energy distance to 10,000 independent target samples.
evaluations.result: MIED has the strongest W2 behavior as dimension rises, while SVGD is better on energy distance; KSDD converges more slowly and exhibits diagonal artifacts in 2D.

evaluations.setting: A linearly transformed product of two heavy-tailed Student-t distributions with 1,000 particles over 2,000 iterations.
evaluations.metric: W2 and energy distance after restricting both sample sets to boxes [-a,a]^2.
evaluations.result: MIED retains the visible heavy tails and becomes better for larger boxes, whereas SVGD is favored on smaller central boxes and fails to cover the tails.

evaluations.setting: Bayesian logistic regression on 13 benchmark datasets with 1,000 particles and 10,000 iterations.
evaluations.metric: Log W2 distance, log energy distance, and test accuracy against 10,000 post-burn-in NUTS samples.
evaluations.result: MIED is best in 8 of 13 W2 cells and 4 of 13 energy-distance cells; test accuracy is similar even for independent MAP-like particle descent, illustrating that accuracy is not a posterior-quality metric.
evaluations.baseline: NUTS reference samples, independent particle descent, SVGD, and KSDD.

evaluations.setting: Uniform sampling on a 2D box, a 20-dimensional Dirichlet target, nonconvex planar constraints, and a sphere-constrained von Mises-Fisher example.
evaluations.metric: W2 distance, energy distance, and qualitative particle coverage.
evaluations.result: MIED is particularly effective on the box and flexible nonconvex constraints; mirrored methods win on the Dirichlet target when supplied with the standard simplex mirror map.
evaluations.baseline: Mirror LMC, SVMD, MSVGD, constrained variants of SVGD and KSDD, and alternate mirror maps.

evaluations.setting: Fair Bayesian neural-network prediction on Adult Income with demographic-parity thresholds.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy versus squared covariance between gender and prediction.
evaluations.result: The displayed MIED runs cover a larger Pareto front than the reproduced trustworthy-constraint baselines, but results are a single plotted sweep without uncertainty estimates or a numeric table.
evaluations.baseline: Methods from Liu et al. 2021, using corrected baseline constraint code; Control+SVGD is omitted after getting stuck at initialization.

limitations: Author-stated: the continuous theory covers full-dimensional or special flat/symmetric lower-dimensional domains, not arbitrary rectifiable manifolds or nonlinear equality constraints.
Author-stated: any fixed positive mollifier bandwidth biases the continuous-energy minimizer away from the target.
Author-stated: the discrete-to-continuous connection is only asymptotic as particle count tends to infinity, with no finite-N approximation bound.
Contradiction audit: the chi-square equality and limiting energy values omit the normalizer Z of unnormalized p.
Contradiction audit: Proposition 3.8 and Assumption A.21 impose support or lower-bound conditions incompatible with the global probability-density setup.
Artifact audit: default code bandwidth semantics, detached diagonal spacing, and the broken ignore-diagonal mode prevent literal reproduction of the displayed mathematical objective.
Reviewer inference: O(N^2) pair interactions, nearest-neighbor search, and full-particle gradients limit scaling; the largest shown posterior experiment uses 1,000 particles.
Reviewer inference: most quantitative synthetic results use low-dimensional targets, hyperparameters are hand-selected, and the fairness comparison lacks repeated-trial uncertainty.
failure_modes: A bandwidth that is too large makes Gaussian-kernel MIED or SVGD collapse into clusters; a bandwidth that is extremely small can become numerically unstable.
A poor reparameterization or mirror map sends finite latent values far from the boundary and prevents adequate boundary coverage.
The finite particle objective has local optima, and convergence of global discrete minimizers does not guarantee gradient descent finds them.
Nearest-neighbor identity changes make the detached diagonal correction nonsmooth and inconsistent with the gradient of the value being logged.
The dynamic barrier's fixed 20 projection sweeps can leave residual violation for many or ill-conditioned constraints.
Targets with zeros, non-smooth log density, nonlinear equality supports, or unknown usable constraint maps fall outside the core assumptions.
Reporting MIE magnitudes across particle counts or target rescalings is misleading when the implementation omits -2 log N and p is unnormalized.
reusable_insights: An approximate identity can convert a local density-ratio functional into pairwise interactions without requiring target samples or its normalizer.
Optimizing the logarithm of a positive energy preserves minimizers while making multiplicative normalizers additive constants and stabilizing gradients.
Sampling objectives need explicit separation of continuous-measure consistency, particle discretization error, and optimizer convergence; proving one does not prove the others.
Constraint handling can be modularized from the sampling force, allowing the same particle objective to use either maps or projected feasible directions.
Artifact audits should test parameter semantics algebraically: whether a code variable denotes bandwidth, variance, or squared bandwidth can change the claimed regime by orders of magnitude.
Exact divergence identities for unnormalized targets should be checked under rescaling; any claimed invariant divergence cannot equal an energy that rescales without a compensating factor.
open_questions: Can the Gamma-convergence theorem be restated and proved with the correct target normalizer throughout?
Can displacement convexity and time-discrete descent be established under assumptions compatible with integrable positive targets on R^n?
What joint rates in particle count, bandwidth, optimization steps, and dimension control error to the target?
Can a differentiable, unbiased diagonal estimator retain the anti-collapse benefit without detaching nearest-neighbor spacing?
Can subquadratic neighbor structures preserve consistency for short-range mollifiers?
How should bandwidth be adapted online without inducing the collapse observed for overly broad kernels?
Do the fairness and complex-constraint advantages persist under repeated trials, stronger constrained MCMC baselines, and exact feasibility checks?

competitive_landscape.title: Sampling with Mirrored Stein Operators
competitive_landscape.difference: Shi, Liu, and Mackey derive SVMD and MSVGD in a mirror-defined dual geometry and provide convergence conditions. MIED avoids requiring a strongly convex mirror map and accepts generic differentiable constraint machinery, but its finite-particle guarantees and artifact fidelity are weaker.

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel Stein Discrepancy Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Korba and colleagues minimize a finite-particle kernel Stein discrepancy with non-asymptotic analysis, but require higher derivatives of log p and target unconstrained Euclidean sampling. MIED uses only first derivatives and adapts readily to constraints through a different interaction objective.

competitive_landscape.title: A blob method for inhomogeneous diffusion with applications to multi-agent control and sampling
competitive_landscape.difference: Craig, Elamvazhuthi, Haberland, and Turanova regularize a weighted porous-medium flow and prove deterministic particle convergence, but their sampling update involves target-density integration and is practical mainly when that integral is tractable. MIED's pairwise energy handles general unnormalized targets more cheaply per interaction.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Rate Free Sampling in Constrained Domains
competitive_landscape.difference: Sharrock and Nemeth combine coin betting with mirrored measure optimization to remove learning-rate tuning across simplex, fairness, and post-selection problems. MIED supports more generic differentiable constraints but retains optimizer, bandwidth, diagonal, and barrier-projection hyperparameters.

competitive_landscape.title: Functional Gradient Flows for Constrained Sampling
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu, Zhu, Ton, and Wynne impose a boundary condition on expressive functional-gradient particle flows and prove continuous-time total-variation convergence. Their boundary integral introduces different numerical costs, while MIED offers a simpler scalar pairwise objective but lacks comparable global convergence to the target for its implemented finite-particle dynamics.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: MIED introduces mollified interaction energies that converge to chi-square divergence and yield one first-order particle sampler for unconstrained and flexibly constrained targets.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The manuscript supplies a variational construction, convexity and Gamma-convergence arguments, Wasserstein differential calculations, an explicit log-domain particle update, two constraint adapters, and experiments spanning synthetic, posterior, simplex, fairness, nonconvex, and spherical targets.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novel and durable contribution is the target-weighted short-range interaction objective plus modular constraint handling, not the exact theorem wording or a uniformly superior sampler. The normalizer error changes all displayed energy identities but leaves target minimizers intact; incompatible optimization assumptions and artifact mismatches prevent treating the implemented dynamics as fully covered by the analysis. Later learning-rate-free and functional-gradient constrained samplers sharpen the competitive standard on tuning and convergence.

reviewer_notes: Read all 32 pages of the exact ICLR 2023/arXiv v2 PDF, including every theorem, displayed equation, proof, table, figure, caption, and appendices A-D; rendered and inspected all pages visually. The official arXiv source archive was checked against the PDF, including compiled inputs and 22 figure assets. The OpenReview PDF/API route is browser-challenged, so the repository's pinned title-exact official arXiv override was used; its PDF and extracted-text hashes were reverified. Artifact audit used the current GitHub main commit df408d263774a693e0f0eb62ccdc9f1a26921827, last pushed 2023-02-28: two commits, no tags/releases, no CI or unit tests, no LICENSE file despite the package classifier, full experiment entry points and datasets, seed helpers, checkpoints, and a Linux/CUDA-pinned 153-package environment. All Python files compile. A direct two-particle smoke check confirmed include_diag='ignore' returns a diagonal-only constant energy and zero gradient. Current official arXiv records for five primary competitors were checked through 2026-08-24.
